cards.explanation: The answer is that they offer to help build the temple. They say, “Let us build with you because, like you, we seek your God…” (Ezra 4:2). That's a hand held out, asking to join the work. I think it sounds friendly, but the next verses show how Zerubbabel, governor of Judah (Haggai 1:1), answers it. Hold onto your oven mitts.

The answer is False. Zerubbabel, Jeshua and the family heads turn the offer down flat. The text says, “You have no part with us in building a house for our God, since we alone must build it for the LORD, the God of Israel, as Cyrus king of Persia has commanded us.” (Ezra 4:3). They say it together, friends, and it's a short answer with no hedging.

The answer is Cyrus. Zerubbabel and the family heads say they must build “…as Cyrus king of Persia has commanded us.” (Ezra 4:3). They don't just say no, friends. They name the king who gave the order. That's like telling a stranger you can't swap the recipe because Mother Miller, who first baked with me, wrote it down.

The answer is that they set out to make Judah afraid to build. The text says the people of the land “…set out to discourage the people of Judah and make them afraid to build.” (Ezra 4:4). Their aim is discouragement and fear. I think that kind of pressure can wear a builder down.

The answer is Darius. Darius king of Persia is where that stretch ends, because the counselors work against Judah “…throughout the reign of Cyrus king of Persia and down to the reign of Darius king of Persia.” (Ezra 4:5). That's a long stretch of kings, friends, and the counselors are at it through all of it.

The answer is Aramaic. The letter “…was written in Aramaic and then translated.” (Ezra 4:7). Bishlam, Mithredath, Tabeel and their associates wrote it to King Artaxerxes. I wrote my first recipe in a language only I could read, so I respect the translation step.

The word is rebellious. Rehum and Shimshai call Jerusalem “…that rebellious and wicked city.” (Ezra 4:12). That's how they describe it in their letter to the king. Those are their words about the city, friends, and they put them in writing.

The answer is their taxes to the king. The letter says if the city is rebuilt, “…they will not pay tribute, duty, or toll, and the royal treasury will suffer.” (Ezra 4:13). Tribute, duty and toll are payments that go to the king. Rehum and Shimshai are talking about his money. If I wanted a king's attention in a hurry, I'd mention the treasury too.

The answer is that he can search his fathers' record books. Rehum and Shimshai say “…that a search should be made of the record books of your fathers.” (Ezra 4:15). They say he'll find in those books that the city is a rebellious city. They hand the king a way to check their claim. That's confident, I'll give them that.

The word is dominion. The letter warns that “…you will have no dominion west of the Euphrates.” (Ezra 4:16). Dominion means the king's rule over that region. That's where Rehum and Shimshai end their warning, friends. It's like closing an email with "URGENT" in capital letters.

The answer is that Jerusalem revolted against kings long ago. The king says, “It was discovered that this city has revolted against kings from ancient times, engaging in rebellion and sedition.” (Ezra 4:19). That's what came back after he issued a decree and a search was conducted. Then look what he builds on it: “…issue an order for these men to stop…” (Ezra 4:21). One report from the search, and the king is ready to give that order.

The answer is True. The king says, “And mighty kings have ruled over Jerusalem and exercised authority over the whole region west of the Euphrates; and tribute, duty, and toll were paid to them.” (Ezra 4:20). He's pointing at Jerusalem's past under those kings. Tribute, duty and toll are part of what he says.

The word is stop. The king says, “Now, therefore, issue an order for these men to stop…” (Ezra 4:21). The order goes to Rehum and Shimshai, and it holds until the king gives another order. One little word, friends, and the whole job hits the brakes.
The answer is False. The king says the city “…will not be rebuilt until I so order.” (Ezra 4:21). He says "until," not "never." It's a pause with a condition attached.

The answer is that they go to Jerusalem and stop the work by force. When the king's letter was read to them, “…they went immediately to the Jews in Jerusalem and forcibly stopped them.” (Ezra 4:23). Rehum, Shimshai and their associates move right away. I think that's a hard moment, friends, and the next verse shows the work ceasing (Ezra 4:24).
